utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honour Judge Mindua. Douglas Stringer with Alexis Demirdjian; intern, Adam Birnbaum; and Case Manager, Thomas Laugel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stringer, I understood that you have something to raise before the witness comes in. Mr. Demirdjian, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Allow me to wish everyone in and around the courtroom a happy new year. I have a practical suggestion to make in relation to the documents that are put in the report of Dr. Nielsen. You have probably seen the exchange of e-mails we've had in the last few days. Now, there are two categories of documents essentially that we're going to be looking at today, documents that are footnoted in the report and documents that are not footnoted in the report which have been shown to the expert in December. Now, in order to keep matters neat, I understand there will be a decision eventually about the admission of these documents. I would suggest that for the documents that are in the report, I will not seek their admission during the examination-in-chief of the witness, whereas documents that are not in the footnotes, that are not in the report, those ones I will seek to tender them, so that at the end of the examination-in-chief when I seek to tender the report and the footnoted exhibits, if there are any arguments, and I believe there will be some, we can keep those that are in the footnotes in one set, one bundle, if I could call it that way. Does that make any sense?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I'm a little bit surprised, Mr. Demirdjian, because I thought that that was exactly what we proposed in the e-mail exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So that means that we agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: We agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: If there is no objection from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honour Judge Mindua. My understanding was that essentially there would be a -- in a sense a formal tender of the documents at the close of the direct examination by the Prosecution and then there would be a subsequent decision by the Chamber, and then we would have an opportunity in the course of -- well, at some stage to make any submissions. So in that sense that was the manner in which I thought it would be carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Unless -- unless I am wrong, but I thought that that particular course of action would only apply to the footnote documents and not to the other ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Mr. President, that was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So we all agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: We do, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And I just wanted to clarify that because I will be displaying these documents that are in the report, I will be showing them to allow the witness to expand. Even when I show them, I will not seek to tender them at that very moment. I will call up the 65 ter number, but I will not seek to tender at that very moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I -- I understand, Mr. Demirdjian. I think in -- in -- it would be helpful, then, if you could indicate that it is a footnoted document --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- that you are showing to the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- so we know that we are not to expect your request to tender it immediately afterwards. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: That's all I had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. The witness may be brought in. And may the record reflect that we sit pursuant to Rule 15 bis, Judge Hall being absent. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Nielsen. Thank you for coming to The Hague to assist the Tribunal. Could you for the record state your name and date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning. Christian Axboe Nielsen, born it 12 September 1973.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have to tell you, you of course already know, that you're going to make the solemn declaration now which exposes you to the penalties of perjury should you give misleading or untruthful evidence to this Tribunal. Could you now please read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Nielsen.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could I to begin ask you a few questions about your professional and educational background before we get into the subject matter of your report. First of all, could you tell the Court what is your current occupation.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: I am currently employed as associate professor of south-east European studies at the University of Aarhus in Denmark.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And while I'm asking you a few questions about the background perhaps we could display Dr. Nielsen's CV which is at 65 ter 3215. That is at tab 27. Doctor, could you tell us a little bit about your educational background, perhaps dealing only with the university level onwards.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: Yes. I did all of my university studies in the United States. I took a bachelors degree in political science and Germanic languages and literatures at Washington University in St. Louis. I then took a master of international affairs degree specialising in human rights and humanitarian affairs in east Central Europe at Columbia University's school of international and public affairs. I then continued on at Columbia University at the graduate school of arts and sciences where I received a Ph.D. in east central European history particularly specialising in the history of Yugoslavia between the two world wars.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And following -- and this was, I believe, your Ph.D. was in -- that would be 1999 -- 2002; is that right? In May of 2002.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. And following your -- your Ph.D., it is correct to say that for a number of years you worked for the Office of the Prosecutor at the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I worked for the Office of the Prosecutor at the ICTY from 2002 until 2004 and then again from 2006 until the end of 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Are you also currently working as a consultant for any other Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: Yes. I am currently working as an external consultant analyst for one of the Defence teams at the Special Tribunal for Lebanon, and I also work as an external expert consultant for the Canadian Department of Justice on cases that their crimes against humanity and war crimes section handles.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Returning now to your current occupation, you explained that you were teaching at the University of Aarhus. What is your area of specialisation?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: I am a historian by training. I specialise in the history of south-eastern Europe or the Balkans with a particular focus on the area that used to be Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And are you currently conducting any research or are you working on any publications?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: Yes. I have a forthcoming publication on the dictatorship of King Aleksandar in Yugoslavia, and I'm currently working on a new research project which involves producing a history of the police in socialist Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And this -- on this last relating to the history of the police, can you expand a bit on what is the subject matter exactly?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: My intent is to write a complete history of the Ministry of Internal Affairs in the socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia from the end of World War II until the collapse of Yugoslavia in 1991, and I am conducting this research as I did with my previous research for the Ph.D. and also research done here at the Tribunal based on archival material that I myself am retrieving from the relevant archives in the former Yugoslavia, in this case in particular the archive of the Republic of Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And prior to working on this research, is it correct to say that you have done other research on police related matters?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I would point out that my dissertation that I wrote at Columbia University was overwhelmingly based on police sources from the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. I then during my years working for the Tribunal focused again primarily on police sources, and in that sense there is a continuity in my current research which also is predominantly focused on police sources and relevant political and other material.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Going specifying to your years working for the Tribunal and the years following that, it is correct that you have testified at the Tribunal on three separate occasions for three separate trials?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: That would be the case of Krajisnik, Stanisic and Zupljanin, and Karadzic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: What was the scope of your reports in those cases?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: In all three cases I focused on the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Serbian Republic in Bosnia and Herzegovina, its establishment and its performance from November 1990 until the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, Dr. Nielsen's CV is not directly footnoted in his report. May I ask to tender 65 ter 3215.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit P364. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Nielsen, I'd like to turn to your report now and to the methodology you applied in preparing this report. Is it correct to say that at the end of the year 2011 you met with members of the Office of the Prosecutor and agreed on terms of reference and the scope of the report which you were to prepare for this trial?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: To be honest, I cannot recall whether I actually met with members of the Office of the Prosecutor at the end of 2011, but I certainly had communications with the Office of the Prosecutor during the course of which I agreed to produce the report which is before us today, and I was given terms of reference on the basis of which I was to produce that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And would it be correct to say that the scope of your reporting included mainly two items, one being the historical and political developments in the former Yugoslavia and Croatia between the years 1990 and 1993, and the second would be to focus on the MUP structures in Croatia during again the years 1991 to 1993, particularly in the Serb entities? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'd like you to explain to the Court how you prepared your report and more specifically how you selected the sources for the preparation of your report.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: I was initially provided with a quite substantial number of documents and also videos by the Office of the Prosecutor. This was a selection that had been made by the Prosecution team. I was invited to review those documents as a way of commencing work on the report. Once I became more familiar with the material that I had been provided with, I then subsequently identified on my own a significant additional number of documents that I wished to examine, and I requested and received all the documents that I thought would be additionally relevant from the Office of the Prosecutor. At several instances, the Office of the Prosecutor of its own volition also identified new material that they deemed relevant for the report, and I was provided with this material and asked to review it to see whether it should be included in my analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now -- and is it correct to say that you were also provided access to the databases of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: Yes, although I did not myself conduct a substantial number of searches on the OTP's databases for the -- for documents relevant to this report. I was in all cases able to identify and obtain when I wanted any relevant additional material. This material was identified by myself largely based on review of the initial batch of documentation which caused me to identify other relevant documents and also by reviewing earlier reports and judgements of this Tribunal that are pertinent, in particular, to the Republika Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. In reviewing this material, would you be reviewing the originals or the translations?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: It is important for me to stress as I have done in previous testimony at this Tribunal that I in all cases conduct my analysis and base my conclusions exclusively on the B/C/S originals of the documents. I speak, read, and write B/C/S fluently, and I in all cases rely on the original documentation as I do in my historical research as well. This also means that I in most cases have not examined, unless I was asked by the Prosecution to do so, any of the relevant translations of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And this is something I may have skipped on your resume. Is it correct to say that you also teach the language?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: Yes. I have also taught B/C/S at the university level in Denmark.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition to the material that you have had access to at the ICTY, did you also use other sources?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: Yes. In addition to the material that I received from the ICTY, I also used a small number of secondary sources, monographs produced by other authors and made limited use of those sources in those cases where the primary source base, that is the documents possessed by the Tribunal, were unable to provide relevant information on, in particular, events that I knew to have happened during this period and which would, in my opinion, have been curiously absent if I had not been able to cite them somehow. Therefore, I made use of a number of works, a number of books, that I myself identified and which we had scanned and ERN'd.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, since we're talking about the use of books published by other authors, there are a few names that come to mind. For example, I've seen that you used the book of Ilija Petrovic, the book published by Nikica Baric, and a chapter of a book published by Caslav Ocic. Can you tell us how you came about to select these books and how much you relied on them?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: I should amend something that I just stated earlier. I consider as an historian and as an analyst the books of Ilija Petrovic and Caslav Ocic - Ocic, excuse me - to be in both cases primary sources. That is how they would be considered by professional historians because they are written by persons who themselves were participants in the events they describe. In the case of Caslav Ocic, he was the Foreign Minister for a time of the Republika Srpska Krajina. He produced what I find to be a quite handy chronology of events in Republika Srpska Krajina, and in the case of Ilija Petrovic, he provides a detailed narrative of political and other events in Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Srem. He was himself a principal participant these events. I should note that in accordance with the professional standards of history and analysis, I weight in my analysis those accounts keeping in mind that those authors themselves have their own subjective points of view, but I have to quite some extent compared their accounts to other documents which bear on similar events and particularly as accords the dating of specific meetings or specific events in Eastern Slavonia and in Krajina as a whole, I find them to be reliable in their recounting of when certain events took place, and it is as such that I have made limited use of those books. In the case of Nikica Baric, he is a Croat historian, a young Croat historian, and I would not normally make use of a book by a Croat historian on what he calls the Serb uprising in Croatia, particularly because of the risk that he has a bias, but I would point out that not only do I make very limited use of this book, again mostly to establish points of chronology, but that Baric's work has been favourably received throughout the former Yugoslavia, and he has published in -- on the RSK in peer reviewed historical journals of the highest order in Serbia and as such is perceived by Serbian historians as being a prominent historian of this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Speaking of a peer review, Dr. Nielsen, could you explain to the Trial Chamber the difference, perhaps, between how a historian would select documents and incorporate in a report as opposed to how lawyers would approach the admissibility of the document?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: Well, at the most basic level I would again come back to this distinction which I think to some extent the court, lawyers, and historians share which is the important distinction between primary sources and secondly sources. Primary sources being documents produced by government institutions, political parties, et cetera, who themselves are actually participating in, as it were, historical events. Here again I include the memoirs correspondence, telephone conversations, whatever else may be accessible, e-mails, of principal actors who themselves participate in the historical events that a court or an historian is examining. I then would mention secondary sources which in most cases are works, scholarly works, or publicistic works which provide second-hand summaries or accounts of these events, and in those cases, of course, I think both historians and lawyers would attach a much lesser weight to those sources not only because those sources to a large extent are informed by hearsay and by subjective considerations of other evidence or source material but because they are themselves also distant in time and place from the original accounts and are not themselves participants in the events. So to that extent, I think particularly as an analyst, as a historian in my work for the Tribunal, I've tried in this report as well to rely as much as possible on primary sources and in particular I would note primary sources produced by the Serbian side in order that we can reduce the inherent bias that would emerge if I were instead to rely on accounts of these events produced by the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And to close on this chapter, Dr. Nielsen, can you explain to the Court the selection you have made of newspaper articles?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: Yes. In a small number of cases in the report, I have used newspaper articles or segments of television shows, what we generally as analysts refer to as open sources. I believe that in the vast majority of cases, I've again availed myself of Serb open sources again to reduce the risk of any bias that might have occurred had I relied instead on Croat open sources from this period. I also rely on a number of interviews that have been published in the Serbian media in particular and which are interviews with principal actors in the RSK or other areas of -- other earlier areas of -- and political structures of the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Speaking of interviews --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: May I have just one moment, please. Dr. Nielsen, you said that: "In particularly I would note that primary sources produced by the Serbian hide in order that we can reduce inherent bias that would emerge if we were instead to rely on accounts of these events produced by the Croats." Could you clarify that for me, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I believe given what is known about the political police and military organs of all sides in the conflict in the former Yugoslavia, particularly in the period from 1990 until 1995 that it would be extremely problematic to write an analytical account of, for example, the police in Serb-controlled areas of Croatia that would rely heavily on Croat sources. Those Croat sources would have a very high interest in portraying the Serbian side and their actions in the most negative light possible, and it would be very difficult for me to be in a position to corroborate whether those Croat sources were actually providing reliable accounts or not. Conversely, I believe that the Serbian/Yugoslav sides in the same period have little logical inherent interest in portraying their own actions negatively. On the contrary, they would have an inherent interest in portraying them more favourably. It follows for me as a point of logic that if the Serb or Yugoslav forces speak of events which they, I believe, are problematic, negative, or detrimental to the security situation, then there is a substantial likelihood that such events did, in fact, occur. For the same reason in dealing with the Bosnian Serb Ministry of Internal Affairs, I relied almost exclusively on the Bosnian Serbs' own documents so as to avoid any bias that was abundantly evident in the documents produced contemporaneously by the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats about the Bosnian Serb police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please proceed, Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Can we display on the screen 65 ter 2130. That's at tab 302.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Just to give an example of a newspaper article that you've selected for the purposes of your report. Dr. Nielsen, I don't know if you are able to see already the B/C/S version on the left side of the screen.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we scroll to the left and up in the B/C/S version so we could see the author and the magazine this was published in. Towards the left, perhaps. Are we able to see this? In the B/C/S version, can we see the left part of the -- the screen. Is that the whole page? Very well?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Nielsen, do you recognise this article?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise this as an interview of Goran Hadzic that I cite in the report. If I maybe of assistance, I believe that the -- in the B/C/S version, the author's name, that is the journalist's name, appears at the end of the article rather than at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Nielsen. Quite right. Now, this is a -- is "Intervju" a magazine or a newspaper?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. As you know, there is an objection that we've made to this document being admitted as an exhibit. Now, of course that doesn't in and of itself preclude hearing Mr. Nielsen on his expert opinions about the content of that proposed exhibit, but I would suggest that if ultimately you decide that this is not admissible, going through this document in detail, hearing its content and having the commentary of Mr. Nielsen -- Dr. Nielsen on these issues would undermine any ultimate ruling that you make on admissibility. So my suggestion would be that we make a decision now on whether or not statements of Mr. Hadzic to a journalist well after the events that are described in the document are going to be admitted by this Chamber before we hear Mr. Nielsen on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know if this will change my learned friend's position -- I'm not sure if this is going to change my learned friend's position, but I do not intend in exploring the newspaper article at this stage. I just want Dr. Nielsen to give us his explanation of how and why he selected this interview and how does he assess the reliability of it. So I will not go into the details or even the substance of the article. I don't know if that changes my learned friend's position on the matter, because we will be strictly relying on this article as a tool reference just to support what is said in the report and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, it's hard for me to understand how he could make any comments about reliability without delving into the content at least to some degree. And our position, to be clear, is that there are not sufficient guarantees or indicia of reliability that the journalist here accurately recorded what Mr. Hadzic may have said to the journalist. It falls well below the standard of what would be deemed admissible by this Chamber under regular circumstances. And bootstrapping it to an expert opinion doesn't change that. In fact, it almost makes it worse. So that's the basis for the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Well just in that case, Your Honours, I believe that it would be -- it would be sufficient for Dr. Nielsen to simply explain why and how he selected the newspaper article, again without going into the substance, and if needs be if there's still a standing objection we will have to see if we can find the journalist if there is really a strong objection about the accuracy and reliability of the article. We can always make investigations to find if the journalist is available, but at this stage it's really about the selection of sources of newspaper articles in relation to -- and there are many more in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed as you indicated you would, Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President. Thank you. I just have a request from my client which I think is a legitimate request. Could we request that the image of Mr. Hadzic's children not be displayed to the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Please proceed, Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Could we go to the last page in the B/C/S version, to the bottom part.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Nielsen, I believe that in the English version we could see what -- the author Gordana Jovanovic. Now, could you explain to us how you came about to select this newspaper article and perhaps explain it to the Judges what your assessment is of it?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: I cannot recall whether this was a document that was provided to me by the OTP or whether I myself requested it. I can comment, however, that the reason I chose to cite it in the report is that this is an interview with the accused, a relevant actor in the context of the RSK and the RSK MUP. The interview stems from "Intervju," which as the name suggests is a Serbian magazine that published a large quantity of interviews with important actors in Serb-controlled areas of Yugoslavia in the mid 1990s. I had the ability in earlier years while working as an analyst to read many issues of "Intervju" and therefore am well familiar with this particular magazine and with the type of interviews and type of persons who were interviewed by the journalists working for this magazine. As an analyst, it is my experience that the interviews -- the content of the interviews in "Intervju" magazine often corresponds quite closely to statements made by those persons interviewed that have been stated publicly by those figures elsewhere on television, in political documents, in political speeches, et cetera. Therefore, as an analyst, I have no reason at present to doubt the veracity of the reporting or transcription, if you will, of the interviews that appear in this magazine, and I do not a priori have any recollections of significant disputes post factum between journalists of this magazine and the persons that they had interviewed regarding the content of these interviews as published.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, Dr. Nielsen, your report was made available at the end of -- well, it was finalised in June and was made available to the Defence at the end of June of 2012. Since then, it is correct to say that you were provided with a collection of new documents; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I was recently provided with a collection of documents from Serbia that had not been available to the Office of the Prosecutor at the time that I produced my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And did you have the opportunity to review some of this material?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. We'll be dealing with them at a later stage. And it is correct to say that in December of last year, in 2012, you met with members of the Office of the Prosecutor for a proofing session at the end of which was prepared an errata sheet; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And in this errata sheet a number of typographical corrections were made; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could we go in private session for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: This closes this chapter of my examination-in-chief, Dr. Nielsen. I would like to now turn to your report. I believe you requested to have a copy available to you. I have a printed copy here. Unless there are any objections, I'd like to make this available to Dr. Nielsen. I will begin with the general historical and political background, and I will move through your report in the order that it is presented in there. I'd like to begin with paragraph 3 where you quote the census, the 1991 census in Croatia, which indicated that out of a population of 4.7 million inhabitants in Croatia, 78 per cent were of the Croatian ethnic background and 12 per cent of the population were of Serbian ethnicity. Just to clarify, you obtained these numbers directly from the census results which were published by the Croatian bureau of statistics; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: Yes, as is indicated in footnote 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And how -- to your knowledge, have these numbers ever been contested or are these numbers accurate?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: To my knowledge, there has been no significant contestation of this number.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, in the census, of course, you have a number of ethnic groups which are listed. You always have Croats, Serbs, ethnic Hungarians, Ruthenians, et cetera, and you also have a part of the population which is named Yugoslavs. Can you tell us to your knowledge how we should assess this -- this -- this term "Yugoslavs"?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: In socialist Yugoslavia there was in the later censuses the possibility of declaring oneself as a Yugoslav rather than as, for example, a Croat or a Serb. Based on my knowledge as an historian, the -- those who identified themselves as Yugoslavs were primarily urban inhabitants of various cities in Yugoslavia, and in a significant number of cases persons who were born out of ethnically mixed marriages and therefore did not wish to choose one ethnicity over the other, but this category of Yugoslavs was never at any time one of the largest categories of self-identification in the Yugoslav censuses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian, just for an error in the -- in the record. It's not me giving evidence here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: If we can move now to paragraph 5 of your report where you discuss the elections in Croatia in April and May of 1990. You refer here to the main political parties such as the HDZ and the SDS, and to support that, I think it is in footnote 4 that you refer again to the book published by Nikica Baric in relation to the seats that were won by the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now if we can perhaps display 65 ter 2578. That is at tab 314. And in the English version I think there are two files. We should display the one that has the ERN 06247029. This is a summary, an English summary which is part of the book. Yes, thank you. Now, in the English summary if we go to page 2, please. Yes. I think it is towards the bottom of the page that Nikica Baric explains that some of the actions of the new Croatian government could not find the support of ethnic Serbs and this is following the -- the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could you explain to us what he is referring to here?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: Well, as I state in paragraph 5, the first multi-party elections that were held in Croatia in 1990 led to the victory of nationalist parties, in particular the quite nationalist Croat Democratic Union or HDZ which obtained the largest percentage of votes and on the other hand, the Serb Democratic Party, the SDS, a nationalist party representing the Serbs in Croatia also received a substantial portion of the vote of Serbs residing in Croatia. Both of these parties portrayed themselves primarily as political organisations that would defend Croat interests in the case of the HDZ and Serb interests in the case of the SDS, and as such they were diametrically opposed and both parties spent a considerable amount of political energy on convincing their respective ethnic populations that -- that they could only find protection and security, political, financial, and economic security if they were gathered on a national basis. In the case of the HDZ, the party and in particular its leader, Franjo Tudjman, on repeated occasions engaged in displays of nationalist symbols, many of which harked back to the so-called Independent State of Croatia, a fascist state that existed from 1941 to 1945, and it was such displays, such rhetoric, among other things, that also led, as Nikica Baric says, ethnic Serbs to severely doubt whether they would have a future in a Croatia, in particular in a Croatia that might be moving towards independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, the very next sentence after the following the one that I quoted earlier says that: "Nevertheless, Serbs used every possibility to show that Croats are endangering them and used this as a pretext for their own aggressive actions." What can you say about this?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: What I can say is that it is my observation of Serb politics in Croatia during this period that they reacted very negatively to the overwhelming victory of the HDZ and the election of Franjo Tudjman as president of Croatia, and as I state in paragraph 6, the anxiety created among the Serb minority in Croatia by this victory was frequently very quickly and later consistently linked to past memories -- excuse me, memories of past oppression of Serbs in Croatia. This -- this anxiety and fear was to a considerable extent manipulated by Serb politicians in Croatia, again as a way of mobilising the Serb ethnic populous in Croatia around the Serb Democratic Party which increasingly portrayed itself as the sole legitimate political representative of Serbs in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, on the basis of documents and books that you have read, what to your knowledge was the position of Serbs in relation to an independent Croatia?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: It is the case that the only previous independent Croatian state that had existed in living memory, if we look at it from the perspective of 1991, was the aforementioned fascist Independent State of Croatia. For that very reason and because of the genocidal politics that the Independent State of Croatia had pursued against the Serb population of Croatia, the very notion of an independent Croatian state was even under the best of circumstances likely to create enormous anxiety among at least a substantial portion of the Serb population in Croatia. As I stated, the inflammable political rhetoric of Franjo Tudjman, who had also as an historian dabbled in revisionism and at times denied the suffering of Serbs in Croatia or at least minimised the suffering of Serbs in Croatia during World War II contributed to the creation of an atmosphere of extreme anxiety among many Serbs in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And was there a -- you said this rhetoric created an anxiety among at least a substantial portion of the Serb population. Was there a portion of the Serb population in Croatia which looked favourably toward an independent Croatia?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: It is difficult to state whether there was any portion of the Serb population that really looked favourably towards an independent Croatia. However, it can probably be stated that among a certain section of Serbs, particularly those living in the larger cities of Croatia, they might possibly have been willing to support more autonomy if not independence for Croatia had the HDZ gone about propagating this policy in a more conciliatory manner. Again, that is, unfortunately, I have to say speculation, because the HDZ did anything but that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. If we move to paragraph 6, you explain here how Serb politicians in Croatia cultivated a fear amongst the Serb minority, that Serbs would be subjected to discrimination, linking this fear to genocide that occurred during the Second World War. Could you tell the Court what is the position amongst academic circles in relation to the assertion that genocide was committed against Serbs during the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: I believe that it is an accurate reflection of the consensus in scholarly circles to state as I do in paragraph 6 of my report that the fascist independent State of Croatia implemented extremely discriminatory policies against Serbs and other minorities, in particular Jews and Roma, in Croatia, culminating in a genocide against the Serbs and these other minorities on the territory of the NDH which we should remember not only incorporated or included the territory of present-day Croatia but also Bosnia-Herzegovina and a substantial portion of Serbia. The policies of the NDH state varied at times in intensity and in particular certain very negative policies pursued by that state such as forced conversions of Serb Orthodox believers to Roman Catholicism varied over time. However, I believe it is an accurate reflection of the state of scholarly knowledge to state that the NDH's policies were absolutely toxic and negative and in some genocidal particularly as concerned the Serb, Roma, and Jewish populations of that state.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: In that paragraph, I think it is at footnote 6 where you referred to a statement made by Milan Martic in an interview in 1994. Perhaps we can display. It's 65 ter 4981, and that is at tab 315. In the footnote you indicate that Milan Martic stated, or referred to a clear indication of the restoration of Nazism from the period 1941 to 1945. And again returning to your comment in paragraph 6 of how Serb politicians used this -- the events the Second World War, what can you make of this statement?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: The statement made by Milan Martic is an accurate reflection of the political rhetoric of Serb leaders in Croatia in the period from the time of the multi-party elections in Croatia and then forward until 1995 in which he and others choose to characterise the newly created -- or the -- excuse me, first the movement to create an Independent State of Croatia and after 1991 the newly Independent State of Croatia as the second coming of the fascist Independent State of Croatia from the Second World War. As I state in paragraph 6, a logical and again unfortunate corollary to this was a choose by many Serb political leaders and some Serbs in the general population of Croatia to refer generically to Croats as the -- as Ustasha, that is the fascist movement that led the Independent State of Croatia to refer to the organs of the Croatian state in Zagreb as Ustasha or NDH organs and again after 1991 to refer to the newly Independent State of Croatia as the NDH. I should note as I do in paragraph 6 that this type of association, discursive association between the Croatian independence movement and the Croatian independent state in the 1990s on the one hand and the fascist Croatian state of the 1940s on the other hand was mirrored on the Croat side by an equally unfortunate tendency by many Croatian media and Croat politicians to refer to Serbs generically as Chetniks, that is, as extreme nationalist Serbs, Chetniks being the royalist nationalist movement that existed during World War II.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Moving on to paragraph 7, Dr. Nielsen, you explain here how in June and July of 1990 the Croatian Serbs begin to contemplate the establishment of self-rule and declare autonomy of the Serb Nation. Now, this took place it would be approximately half a year before the adoption of the new constitution in Croatia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, did you say approximately half a year before or after a year --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Half a year before.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And just to be clear, when was the new Croatian constitution adopt?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: It was promulgated on the 22nd of December, 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, it appears though that at this time some constitutional changes were already proposed by the summer of 1990. Perhaps if we could look at tab 8. That's 65 ter 50, 5-0. Again, this is a document which is in your report. It is a press report from Tanjug, from the 31st of July, 1990. And it states here that in line with the decision by the recent gathering a Serb referendum would be held. Towards the end of this article the paragraph before the last one, it reads here: "At today's session the Serbian National Council rejected all amendments to the constitution of the Croat republic adopted by the Croat Assembly. The council also rejects the use of Croat national symbols, especially the coat of arms," et cetera. Although the constitution was adopted in December of 1990, it appears that already in the summer of 1990 some constitutional changes were already in the works. Now, generally what was the position of the Serb politicians in relation to these constitutional changes?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: The position of the Serb Democratic Party was certainly negative as regarded the proposed changes which would lead or pave a path towards Croatian independence and towards any constitutional changes which might certainly in the eyes of the Serbs lead to a diminishing or erasure of their status as a constituent nation of Croatia as they -- a constitutional status that they had enjoyed until 1990. So in this case, what we see is that the drafting of the new constitution is obviously a longer procedure which is discussed in the Sabor or parliament in Croatia and that the Serbs are already at this stage expressing quite serious concerns about where this is all headed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, at paragraph 7 you explain that a referendum was held in relation to Serbian autonomy, and you cite the report of the central commission which was overseeing the vote. This is at 65 ter 59, at tab 12. We can display that for a moment. Yes. Now, could you -- could you tell us how you view the result here whereby 567.127 persons voted for Serbian autonomy versus 144 who voted against? How do you review this result?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: Well, what we see in this period both in Croatia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina are moves by ethnic Serb political parties, in both cases in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina called the Serb Democratic Party, to stake out their political positions which were against increased autonomy or independence for Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. One of the ways in which these parties mobilised political support and publicised their opposition to moves towards Croatian or Bosnian independence was by holding such referenda. This referendum for example in Croatia is pretty much a self-selective referendum. Anyone who is likely to participate in this referendum organised by the Serbs in Croatia is likely to vote yes. Anyone who opposes it is not likely to participate in the referendum. And it is also for this reason that as I state in paragraph 8 the authorities in -- of the republic of Croatia regarded this referendum as informal and also illegal and attempted to stop it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: If we return to page 1 in the English version, under item 2 we see the municipalities which towards the bottom of the page, if we could zoom in on the -- yeah. Thank you. We can see the municipalities where the vote was held. We see Knin, Benkovac, et cetera, and in the fourth line we can see that some municipalities in Eastern Slavonia and Baranja, namely Beli Manastir and Vukovar, also participated in this -- this referendum. I'm mentioning this because I'd like to tie this to the next document, which is P62.50. This is at tab 334. It's a report from a police station. This is a document, actually, that is not in your report, but I believe you've had a chance to look at it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we display it on the screen, please. Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, we can see on the top left-hand corner Djakovo public security station. I don't know -- I haven't asked you this before, but do you know where Djakovo is exactly?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Djakovo is located in Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And it appears here that if we look at this report, that the Croatian police did try to interfere, as it is indicated in your report, during this referendum. You were mentioning just a few moments ago that this was a self-selective report -- referendum. Can you gather anything from this police report in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: Well, I would first remark that in the previous document we saw the list of municipalities. They're -- and in some cases portions of municipalities conforms to those areas in which there were substantial if not majority Serb populations. So that again shows that this was not a country-wide referendum but, rather, a referendum that was conducted first and foremost in areas where the Serb population in Croatia was concentrated. Looking at the document in front of us, we see that there are individuals who have been using their own vehicles and essentially volunteering in order to organise informally this referendum where they go around to villages in various municipalities and sit down with persons, Serbs whom they regard as being favourably predisposed towards organising this and holding this referendum. These persons were then charged with identifying other Serbs in their municipalities and villages, et cetera, and mobilising them to vote in this referendum so that the result could be as considerable as possible. I would note that both in this document and the document I refer to in paragraph 8, the hostility of the authorities of the Republic of Croatia and in particular the deployment of Croatian police to try to confiscate ballots or in other ways obstruct the referendum in some ways seems to have functioned as confirmation in the minds of some Serbs that the Croatian police was indeed aiming to act in ways that were against the interests of Serbs in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And we see at the third -- in the third paragraph here the very last sentence when they're discussing Veljko Brkovic's activities, the last sentence reads: "For this purpose he planned to visit Serbian majority villages." Does that match with your understanding of how the referendum was held?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, if we move to -- if we skip to paragraph 14 of your report, you explain that various developments took place during the spring of 1991, including a referendum which was held by Croatian Serbs on the 12th of May. This is at 65 ter 150, which is tab 48 in the list. If we could display this -- this document, please. And I think it is correct to say that during this referendum, again a very large majority of the people were leaving - and in this case this is in the SAO Krajina - voted in favour of remaining in Yugoslavia. Now, before we get into the document itself, is it correct to say that during the same month the government of Croatia held its own referendum on independence?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: All right. And that Croatia declared its independence a month later, on the 25th of June; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. And looking at this document, could you again comment on the municipalities which -- where this referendum was held.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: Well, the municipalities we see on the list here are the municipalities in what is known as -- as the Krajina region of Croatia, which is a historical region that had existed for several centuries and in which, therefore, a number of again historical reasons was a very, very significant Serb population and indeed a majority Serb population. So it is these municipalities and this region known as the Krajina that becomes the driving force in the organisation of the Serbs in Croatia. It should be pointed out as a point of general interest that a very large number of Serbs in Croatia were sighted in major cities such as Zagreb, Karlovac, Osijek, Split, and so on, and that in many cases these Serbs numerically constituted larger groups than the sum population of the sparsely populated Krajina municipalities, but it was these rural municipalities where the Serbs constituted a solid majority that, as I said, were the driving force in the organisation of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Well, in relation to that, under number 10 we see Knin. Could you perhaps describe to the Trial Chamber how important of a city Knin was before the beginning of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: Knin is a city that is located in a rural part of the Dalmatian Krajina, and I think could safely -- it could safely be said that Knin in no way prior to 1991 was a place that figured prominently in the popular mind of residents of the Republic of Croatia. It is a much smaller town than the primary urban settlements in Croatia and in the context of policing was subordinate to the more significant population centre of Sibenik.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: All right. And before we break, I would like to ask you a question relating to paragraphs 15, 16, and 17, because here we see you mentioning Milan Martic, who was at the time secretary of the SAO Krajina SUP. Paragraph 16, we see that he's appointed as the minister of defence of the SAO Krajina. This is on 29th of May, 1991. And if we flip to paragraph 17, and this is about a month later, he's also -- here it says re-appointed as minister of internal affairs of the SAO Krajina. Could you explain perhaps to the Trial Chamber this accumulation of titles?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to explain the accumulation of titles other than to state that it is clear that Milan Martic in -- who was one of the most prominent police officers in Knin, again was perhaps the actor who played the leading role in organising the police structures in Krajina. This -- perhaps we could explain the conglomeration or accumulation of titles by noting that Martic and other members of the police in Knin and in the SAO Krajina regarded the police as the most proximate reliable and useful line of defence against possible movements to put down attempts at establishing Serbian autonomy in the Krajina, and in that sense it follows logically that the police not only would be a force for internal affairs as it has traditionally been in socialist Yugoslavia, but also a force that could be part of a nascent defence effort and hence the title of minister of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Nielsen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will be moving to a new chapter, so this may be an appropriate time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Demirdjian. Dr. Nielsen, this is the time for our first break. We'll come back at 11.00. You will be escorted out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Nielsen, I would like to turn to section B of your report dealing with the establishment of the SAO SBWS. You indicate at paragraph 18 that a referendum was held on autonomy for Serbs in August and September 1990, and then at paragraph 19, you deal with the creation of the Serb National Council in the SAO SBWS. Now, at paragraph 20, you describe the content of the declaration of sovereign autonomy of the Serb Nation and the SBWS. This is P81.50 at tab 143. Can we perhaps display this. P81.50. Yes, thank you. Now, we see the declaration on sovereign autonomy of the Serb people of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. Could we go to the next page in the English versions and take a look at the items 7 and 8, please. Right. Here we see that the establishment -- this discusses the duties of the Serb National Council, and I would like you to comment, Dr. Nielsen, on what the nature of this -- was the nature of this body, the Serb National Council. How are we supposed to view it in the context of the events in early 1991?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: Well, what we see here is a process that first started in the area called the SAO Krajina and which was later emulated in the area of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem and also separately in the area of Western Slavonia in which the Serb people led by -- primarily by the Serb Democratic Party mobilised in response to what they viewed as Croatia's and Croat politicians' drive towards increasing autonomy and independence for Croatia. What this results in can most neatly be summarised under the saying: Why should we end up being a minority in your country if you can potentially end up being a minority in our country? That is to say the Serb politicians as we saw already with the referendum are identifying those portions of Croatia in which the Serbs constitute a demographic majority. They are proclaiming autonomous districts in those areas and establishing of their own volition institutions such as the Serb National Council here in January 1991 which they view as the sole legitimate political representatives of the Serbs in those areas of Croatia. Legally speaking, with a happens during this period is that the Serbs go from, as we see in the document before us, stating that they will disregard any legislation coming from Zagreb that conflicts with the constitution of Yugoslavia or in any way negatively affects the interests of Serbs in Croatia to a later phase in which they again reassert the primacy of federal Yugoslav legislation until they finally after the independence of Croatia state that they regard all legislation stemming from Croatia and all regulations as null and void. So this is an attempt at politically, legally and ultimately also militarily and in a police sense organising the Serbs to defend their interests against what they see as this hostile emerging independence Croatian state.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Well, in terms of the territory where this autonomy was to be exercised, I think under item 9 we could see that this decision indicates or this declaration indicates that the autonomy was to be, how would I say, exercised over a territory where Serbs have majority now and where they had majority on April the 6th, 1941. Could you explain to the Court what is the significance of this date?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: Well, in April 1941, Nazi Germany, together with several of its allies in the axis forces, commenced an armed attack against the then Kingdom of Yugoslavia, and in the course of this attack, Yugoslavia quickly capitulated and the aforementioned Independent State of Croatia was established. As I also mentioned as a matter of historical consensus it can be said that the Independent State of Croatia implemented a genocidal policy against the Serbs which had very detrimental effects for the Serb population of Croatia. So what we see here, and I mention this in paragraph 20 of my report, is an assertion by Serb politicians in Croatia that they not only wish to provide autonomy and ethnically based political representation for Serbs where they are currently a majority but also in a way as they see it rectify the historical injustice of the genocide and therefore incorporate areas where Serbs were already -- were a majority in 1941, that is, before the establishment of the Independent State of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. I would like to display a video which you refer to in your report. This is 65 ter 4804, and I'd like to play the first clip which starts from the beginning of the video and ends at about the 1-minute mark. We can play it now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] A member of the National Council, Ilija Koncarevic, the General-Secretary, Pero Matic, professor from Beli Manastir, Slavko Dokmanovic, resident of the municipality of Vukovar, Goran Hadzic, the president of the Municipal Board of the Serbian Democratic Party of Vukovar, and a member of the Main Board of the SDB of Knin and Caslav Ocic from Dalj. The Serbian National Council for Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem was set up this year in Sidski Banovci, on Orthodox Christmas. Only the name of the General-Secretary Ilija Koncarevic was known and tonight we identify another member, that's Ilija Petrovic. Mr. Petrovic, tell us, is it --"

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Nielsen, first of all, have you seen this footage before?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: Yes, this is one of the videos that I reviewed in the course of preparing my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And having reviewed this video before, could you tell the Court -- the names were mentioned, but could you tell the Court who we have seen, who were introduced in this -- in this show?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: Well, we have a number of people here, Pero Martic, Slavko Dokmanovic, Goran Hadzic, Caslav Ocic. These, as the speaker says -- and Ilija Petrovic is there as well who is the author of the book which I avail myself in -- in footnote 45 where this video is also cited. These are the principal actors at least those who were public -- ready to appear in public at this time who were involved in establishing the Serb National Council of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. Mr. Petrovic makes mention in his book of the fact that a considerable portion of the initial political organisation was done covertly and therefore not everyone involved in this process was ready to appear publicly in a television appearance such as this at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. And can we play the second clip, which starts at the 51 minutes mark, 51.53.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Anchor: By bringing this show to an end, let's ask Mr. Koncarevic, the Secretary-General of the Serbian National Council for Baranja and Western Srem, what is your view of a solution for Serbia? "Mr. Koncarevic: I'm somehow limited by the views of the Serbian National Council in this evening's broadcast. We have today adopted a position as regards the solution to this problem that we shall forward to the Presidency. There is disputable and indisputable territories in Croatia. The indisputable territory is the territory where Croats were ethnic majority before the beginning of the World War I. Indisputable, that is disputable territory, is the one in Krajina and Western Srem, Baranja, Slavonia and Moslovina. We propose that Yugoslav Presidency suspend the authority of the Croatian Sabor and Croatian leadership in all territories where Serbian people live. This because elementary human rights of Serbian people have been jeopardised and one has elementary right to live. This right has been threatened. Furthermore --"

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, here Ilija Koncarevic discusses disputable and undisputable territory in Croatia. Can you comment on that, again tying into the document we just saw before?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: This is a statement which reflects the general sentiment among the politicians who -- and others who were involved in creating the Serb National Council of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem and, in fact, also reflects the thinking of those involved in creating the other SAOs that were emerging in Croatia at the time, that there were historical areas that were so to say undisputably Serb and that those areas needed to be included in any political reorganisation of Croatia under Serb or Yugoslav control. And again we see the notion that these territories are defined in, if you will, a historical way that is not just based on contemporaneous demographical data but also based on the Serbs' understanding of areas in which they had, historically speaking, particularly before World War II and in some cases before World War I, constituting -- constituted a majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, we see Ilija Koncarevic here, and earlier we also saw Ilija Petrovic. You mention them in your report. Could you tell the Court what was their role from the documents that you have seen during 1991?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: Well, these two gentlemen were among the most prominent actors in organising the Serbs politically in the area of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, and they became part of the Serb National Council and were prominently involved in drafting its policies, and as I noted, that is one of the reasons why I rely in no small -- to no small extent on, in particular, the member -- the memoirs of Ilija Petrovic, who was a member of the Executive Council and whose account is generally corroborated by documents such as the Gazetted declaration that we saw earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, at paragraph 21, you describe how Goran Hadzic was appointed as president of the Serb National Council on the 17th of March, 1991. And then at paragraph 22, you explained the decision whereby the SBWS joined the Vojvodina on the 31st of March, 1991. And just to clarify this for the Judges, where is Vojvodina located exactly?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: First, I would just like to state as pertains to paragraph 21 and the appointment of Mr. Hadzic as president of the Serb National Council, it should be noted that Mr. Petrovic in his account states that it took quite some time and effort on his part and on the part of other Serbs in the area of Eastern Slavonia to persuade in Hadzic to take an active political role. So that, I think, is relevant for the Court to know. As regards Vojvodina, Vojvodina is an autonomous area -- or autonomous region within the Republic of Serbia, roughly speaking the area north of the Danube, and it is the area that is contiguous with Eastern Slavonia. This is one -- if -- and perhaps the first effort in the declarations of the politicians, the Serb politicians in Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem to amalgamate themselves with the -- either the Republic of Serbia or in this case the autonomous region of Vojvodina. Again this is an expression that if the Croats were to move towards a succession from -- of a secession, I should say, from the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, then the Serbs would wish to find some way to remain within Yugoslavia, and one of the ways to do this was to amalgamate with Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. In relation to that, I think at paragraph 23 you refer to a letter which was sent by the Serb National Council to the SFRY Presidency about the deterioration of the situation, and I think it is Petrovic who signs this document where he writes that all Croatian police stations have drawn up lists of Serbs who were to be arrested or killed. This is again at paragraph 23 of your report. How would you qualify this statement?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: I would qualify this as a statement that is indicative of the perceptions, some would argue misperceptions, of the Serbs in terms of what they could expect from the police in Croatia, that is, the police controlled by the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Republic of Croatia. There were a number of important symbolic and other changes of nomenclature undergoing in the police of Croatia at this time. For example, the shift from the word "milicija," which had been used in socialist Yugoslavia to characterize the uniformed police to "policija." Also the use of certain other Croatian words which led Petrovic and others to the conclusion that what they were witnessing was the re-establishment of an ethnic Croatian police force that potentially would resurrect the very negative and persecutory policies of the Independent State of Croatia during the Second World War. So when Petrovic as a responsible and leading politician in the area expresses this, this is something that people would listen to and which would contribute to the increase in anxiety and insecurity that was informing the area and the population at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, just in passing, at paragraph 25 you describe there the events on the 25th of June which we've heard plenty of evidence about before this Court. I would like to skip to paragraph 32 of your report whereby you state here that on the 23rd of August, the Serb National Council proclaimed a general mobilisation in SBWS, and perhaps if we could display 65 ter 01939, and that is the -- at tab 292. That is the book by Ilija Petrovic. And if we could go in the B/C/S version to the page 360. Thank you. I believe we have an English translation. Maybe it's there as a separate file. While the English version is being pulled up, Dr. Nielsen, can you tell us in the B/C/S whether this is the right -- the correct page in relation to the general mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. I'm not entirely sure this is the right page in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If I may assist, it should be somewhere after page 23 of the English translation. I don't have an exact reference, but it should be --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- in that range.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page. I apologise for that, Your Honours. I believe there is a separate translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Just for the record, there are two English translations attached to this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we go to the other English file, please. Okay. We will return to this once we have located the correct page. I apologise for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Nielsen, we will come back to this paragraph, but for now I'd like to take you to paragraph 37. Now, in the preceding paragraphs, 35, 36, we start seeing a certain amount of legislative activity in the SAO SBWS, and we see the appointment of several members of the government, and on the 9th of October, we see a law on the government is adopted. Now, you indicate at paragraph 37 that as -- as of that moment, the government replaced the Serb National Council. Just to clarify this, was the government -- was there any governmental activity prior to the 9th of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: Yes, there was. As I indicate in the preceding chapter -- excuse me, paragraphs, there were a number of things going on. For example, in paragraph 36, the establishment of staffs and units of civil protection by the government of the Serb district of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. I have to state as a point of information to the Chamber that it is my experience as an analyst that both in the SAO Krajina and also in the SAO of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem there was a great deal of inconsistency in the terminology used during this period in terms of whether one or another thing was being done by, for example, the Great National Assembly, the government, or the Serb National Council, and that sometimes creates a bit of confusion in trying to figure out exactly which body was doing what, but according to Ilija Petrovic, as of the 9th of October, the government replaced the Serb National Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, in the next paragraph you mention that a decision was adopted to -- by the Great National Assembly to formally merge the Territorial Defence of the SBWS with the armed forces of the SFRY. Could you tell us based on the documents you have seen what was the JNA's perception of the emerging government in the SAO SBWS?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: This is an excellent question and it is in many ways contingent in the sense that it depends on which JNA officers one looks to in terms of their own documents on the SAOs during this period. It can be generally said that the JNA's policy during this period is evolving in a way that they regard the attempts of the Serbs to -- of Croatia to organise themselves and to protect themselves against a Croatian polity that is moving towards independence as a legitimate process and therefore are willing to extend logistical and other assistance to the Serbs of Croatia in their organisation and their self-defence. Again, this is because the JNA has -- the Yugoslav People's Army was obviously doctrinally and legally obliged to protect the territorial integrity of Yugoslavia, and henceforth -- or, hence, many in the JNA, if not most at this time, particularly officers from Serbia and Montenegro, and Serbs, officers from other parts of Yugoslavia, viewed Croatia and Slovenia's move toward independence as an illegal or hostile act. It should also be noted, however, that in a number of contemporaneous JNA documents, JNA officers, including officers of the security organs of the JNA refer to the Serb autonomous districts that are being established in Croatia as self-proclaimed and sometimes list the names of these districts in quotation marks, thereby indicating at the very least a skepticism as regards their legal legitimacy. Over time the JNA particularly after the declaration of independence of Croatia in June 1991 tends to regard the SAOs in a much more favourable way and lend much more overt assistance to them. * Q. On that topic, could I ask that we display 65 ter 6022 at tab 337. This, Your Honour, is a document that is not in Dr. Nielsen's report. It is part of the collection which was obtained after the preparation of his report. And, Dr. Nielsen, this is a document from the command of the 12th Corps on the 8th of November, 1991, from the village of Dalj. Do you remember having reviewed this document before?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. It does deal a bit with the police, and we will deal * with the police in a moment, but I would like you to look at the first dash, if that were to -- yeah. Perhaps the fourth paragraph in the B/C/S version. And you can see here that the 12th Corps in fact is sending this to the 1st Military District, which is its higher command and is requesting some clarification. Can you comment on that -- on that first sentence here in this first dash.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN AXBOE NIELSEN
utterances.text: Yes. This is a military document from this period in the autumn of 1991 where we see that a portion of the military is -- of the JNA is clearly still struggling to come to terms with what the exact legal status or authorities of the Assembly of the Serb district of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem and the government of that district are. That is, as they say, have they established their legal legitimacy? Are they international recognised?
